explanations.answer: On the grace coming when Jesus Christ is revealed
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Peter says to "Set your hope fully on the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ." Notice the word fully. He doesn't say save a little hope for the oven and a little for the bank account. All of it goes in one place.

explanations.answer: On the day their years of hardship finally end
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd pick it, because hard seasons make us all watch the calendar. But Peter points their hope somewhere else: "…the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ." He says to set it fully there. A hope that's tied to the day the hard stuff stops is a little too small for what Peter hands them.

explanations.answer: On the reward their faithful work will earn them
explanations.explanation: Close to the neighborhood, friend, but not quite the address. Peter says their hope goes on "…the grace to be given you…" and grace is a gift, so nobody earns it with a punch card. It's given at the revelation of Jesus Christ. I've stamped a lot of cookies and not one of them paid for a gift like that.

Not quite, friend. Peter says the opposite: "As obedient children, do not conform to the passions of your former ignorance." He doesn't want them copying that old pattern. Think of an old recipe that never once turned out right, and why would you keep following it?

Yep, it's False. Peter says, "As obedient children, do not conform to the passions of your former ignorance." So he's telling them not to let those old passions press their shape onto them anymore. Don't be the cookie that goes back into the old mold.

explanations.answer: Because the One who called them is holy
explanations.explanation: There it is, baker. Peter says, "…just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do…" and then points to Scripture: "Be holy, because I am holy." The reason isn't a rule list. It's who called them. When the One who calls you is holy, that's the whole reason.

explanations.answer: Because their neighbors are watching them closely
explanations.explanation: Peter never says a word about neighbors watching. His reason is "…He who called you is holy…" and he backs it up with "Be holy, because I am holy." This isn't about putting on a show for the people next door. It's about the One who called them.

explanations.answer: Because being holy keeps their troubles away
explanations.explanation: I'd sign up for that deal, friend, but Peter doesn't offer it. His reason is simple: "…He who called you is holy…" and it is written, "Be holy, because I am holy." The reason points at God, not at an easier week. Holy isn't a trouble repellent.

That's right. Peter says, "Since you call on a Father who judges each one’s work impartially, conduct yourselves in reverent fear…" Reverent means they take Him seriously and honor Him. It's the kind of respect where you stand up straighter when the Father walks in the room.

I like easy comfort as much as the next stamper, but that's not what Peter says. He says to conduct themselves "…in reverent fear…" since their Father judges each one's work impartially. Peter wants them to take the Father seriously. This isn't a slouch-on-the-couch kind of verse.

Nice and loud, friend, but Peter picks a different word. He says to conduct themselves "…in reverent fear…" because their Father "…judges each one’s work impartially…" Fear that's reverent means honoring Him with a serious heart. Bold confidence is a fine phrase, just not the one on this page.

You got it, baker. Peter says to conduct themselves in reverent fear "…during your stay as foreigners." That fits how he opens the letter, writing to God's chosen people scattered across places like Pontus and Galatia (1 Peter 1:1). A foreigner knows this isn't home, and I know a little about being far from the kitchen.

Good word, but it's not the one Peter uses. He says "…during your stay as foreigners." A stay is a temporary visit, the way you'd stay at a hotel and not move in. Servants is a different picture altogether.

Rulers would be a big promotion, friend, but Peter's word is "foreigners." He says to live in reverent fear "…during your stay as foreigners." Nobody's handing out crowns in this verse. These are people staying somewhere that isn't home.

That's True, baker. Peter says, "…it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed…" Silver and gold are the things you'd expect to pay with. Peter says that's not what bought them back, and he tells us what did in the next verse.

Peter really does say it, friend. "…it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life…" So the statement is True. Silver and gold are perishable, and Peter says they didn't buy this.

That's the answer. Peter says they were redeemed "…with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot." Precious is Peter's word for it, and it fits. Not silver, not gold, but the blood of Christ.

Not what Peter says, friend. He says they were redeemed "…with the precious blood of Christ…" Peter doesn't mention priests or their offerings here at all. It's Christ's own blood, and nothing else on the list.

That's not what Peter points to, friend. He says they were redeemed "…with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot." Prayers of the prophets don't come up in this verse. It's one answer, and it's Christ. Peter keeps the spotlight right on Him.

explanations.answer: In the last times for their sake
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. Peter says Christ "…was known before the foundation of the world, but was revealed in the last times for your sake." Your sake means the very people Peter is writing to. I think that's worth a pause, because it's personal.

explanations.answer: In the days of Moses for Israel's sake
explanations.explanation: Good guess if you're thinking of big moments in Israel's story, but Peter says something different. Christ "…was revealed in the last times for your sake." Moses isn't in this verse. The timing is the last times, and the sake is theirs.

explanations.answer: At the very beginning for the angels' sake
explanations.explanation: Peter does mention the beginning, but only for when Christ was known: "…before the foundation of the world…" Then he says Christ "…was revealed in the last times for your sake." Angels don't come up in this verse. It's the last times, and it's for the people reading Peter's letter.

You got it, baker. Peter writes, "…your faith and hope are in God." He says it right after telling them God raised Christ from the dead and glorified Him. So their faith and hope rest on the God who did that.

Wisdom is a great thing to have, friend, but it's not Peter's word. He says, "…your faith and hope are in God." That comes right after he says God raised Christ from the dead and glorified Him. Hope is the word that finishes the line.

Strength sounds right, since we all need some on a long baking day. But Peter's word is hope: "…your faith and hope are in God." God raised Christ from the dead and glorified Him, and that's what Peter ties their faith and hope to. Strength isn't in the line.

explanations.answer: Love one another deeply from a pure heart
explanations.explanation: That's the command, baker. Peter says, "…love one another deeply, from a pure heart." They've purified their souls by obedience to the truth so they'd have genuine love, and now he tells them to use it. Love like that has to get out of the box and onto the counter.

explanations.answer: Keep their love within their own households
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't draw a fence like that. He says, "…love one another deeply, from a pure heart." One another points at the whole group of believers he's writing to, and not just whoever lives under one roof. Love that stays in one kitchen isn't what he's asking for.

explanations.answer: Share their love with those who love them back
explanations.explanation: That's an easy kind of love, friend, and Peter doesn't limit it. He says, "…love one another deeply, from a pure heart." Nothing in the line says to wait and see who loves them first. Jesus asked a harder question about that kind of love, too (Matthew 5:46).

explanations.answer: The living and enduring word of God
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Peter says they've been born again "…through the living and enduring word of God." Living and enduring, both at once. Peter even sets it against "perishable seed," and says this seed is imperishable (1 Peter 1:23).

explanations.answer: The faithful work of the apostles
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd pick it, but that's not what Peter names. He says the new birth came "…through the living and enduring word of God." The word is what does it. Peter doesn't point to the people who brought the message here. He points to the word.

explanations.answer: The long line of their forefathers
explanations.explanation: Nope, and Peter actually goes the other way. He says the empty way of life was something "…you inherited from your forefathers…" (1 Peter 1:18). The new birth is "…through the living and enduring word of God." Family tree one way, word of God the other.
Not in this verse, friend. The Scripture says, "the grass withers and the flowers fall…" Grass and flowers don't last, and that's the whole point. What lasts comes in the very next line.

Yes, it's False. The Scripture says, "All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall…" They fade and drop. I'm glad the verse puts the glory part in there, because I was a little worried about my mustache.
That's it, baker. The Scripture says, "…the word of the Lord stands forever." Grass withers, flowers fall, and the word is still standing. That's the one thing in the whole picture that doesn't fade.

That's what the grass does, friend, not the word. The Scripture says the grass withers and the flowers fall, "…but the word of the Lord stands forever." That "but" is a hinge. Everything before it fades and the word doesn't.

The text doesn't say anything like that. It says, "…the word of the Lord stands forever." Then Peter adds, "…this is the word that was proclaimed to you." It's out in the open, and it was told to them.
